newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans have "positive" budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans have "positive" budget talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton met with the Republican leaders of Congress on Tuesday to discuss balancing the budget and both sides emerged from the talks singing a chorus of cooperation and goodwill.

One week after voters re-elected Clinton but left both houses of Congress under Republican control, Clinton met with top Republicans to lay out his agenda for his second term, notably balancing the budget and reforming campaign finance.

In what seemed like a peace offering to the Republicans before the meeting, Clinton eased his opposition to a constitutional amendment to balance the budget -- a top Republican goal the president once derided as a "gimmick."

Speaker of the House of Representatives Newt Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and House Majority Leader Dick Armey, all Republicans, told reporters after the meeting that it was positive, constructive and amicable.

But whether this initial burst of goodwill will overcome the vitriol of the election campaign just ended and translate into actual legislative achievements, rather than gridlock, remained open to question.

"I thought we had a very positive meeting, looking at how we can solve problems next year. I think there's a real desire on the part of everybody to find a way to spend a year really working on solutions," said Gingrich.

"We covered a very wide range of topics and I think that on most of them we agreed that if we're careful and get it done in a practical, positive, problem-solving way, that we can probably get a great deal done," he added.

Lott, who suggested over the weekend that the Republicans were still smarting from Clinton's campaign attacks on them -- notably on the Medicare health care programme for the elderly -- also sought to accentuate the positive.

"We were able to cooperate a great deal in the last two months of the last session, even with an election under way we produced a lot of really good legislation the American people wanted so we have a model of how to ge the job done," he said.

In the one sign of Republican caution amid an otherwise unrelieved chorus of optimism, Lott suggested he would leave to Clinton the thorny task of proposing ways to reform Medicare, an extremely popular programme among the elderly.

"The president will need to make it clear that we have important and tough decisions we need to make in that area," Lott said. "When he lays out the problem and suggests a solution, we're certainly going to be prepared to work with him."
Democratic House Minority Leader Dick Gephart also left the talks upbeat, saying both sides agreed that balancing the budget and reforming the campaign finance system were top priorities.
"There was a spirit there that suggests that the bipartisan work of balance the budget can proceed," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry.

Before the meeting, Clinton told reporters he could accept a balanced budget amendment if it were flexible enough to cope with a recession, a gesture to the Republicans and an acknowledgment of political realities.
The Republicans, who have championed the idea since Ronald Reagan was president, gained two seats in the Senate in the election, making it all but certain the amendment will pass.
In the last Congress, the amendment passed the Republican House of Representatives overwhelmingly, but failed by one vote in the Senate.
"I just want to make sure that if we have one ... it needs to clearly give us the possibility of dealing with a recession," Clinton told reporters at the White House in the morning.

"We don't want to wind up with a Congress some day in a recession raising taxes or throwing unemployed people off health care because we're trying to reach a balanced budget. You could actually wind up making the deficit worse."
